title: The Sunstone Pendant's Secret
markdown:
In the high valley archipelago of Aeridor, rope ferries slept between the crags and bells found one another through fog. Edda moved like water that had learned manners. Her gaze measured distance the way a peak measures weather. On her shoulder, Rook kept the older secrets: a raven whose mind was brighter than the wet shine on his feathers, a sentinel of the winds that came down from places maps refused to name.

Their days had a quiet grain. They polished blades until the steel held the mountain without comment. They tended moonpetal beds that opened only when twilight made up its mind. Between elf and bird there was a language that did not bother with syllables. Peace, being peace, did not last.

It began at the Shrine of the Whispering Stones, a place Edda visited because few others did. Traders arrived instead, carts loud with silk and spiced wine, and they mistook her stillness for rank. They pressed a warm stone into her palms before she could assemble a refusal dignified enough for the mountain. The pendant held sunlight the way a jar holds honey: pulsing, slightly too pleased with itself. The Sunstone Pendant, they said, a gift for a noble visitor. Edda accepted with a nod that meant she would rather not make a scene. Rook’s silence, for once, sounded like a sigh.

The pendant was not a trinket. It was said to keep Aeridor’s pacts: prosperity, unity, the mountains’ good temper. Edda’s judgment, which could unpick a lie faster than frost finds a puddle, did not trust the traders’ flourish. She needed a wizard who knew old things, even if that wizard loved his wardrobe more than his books. With Rook riding the highest current of her cloak, she climbed to the crooked tower of Wizard Elmsworth, where the clouds had to step aside.

Elmsworth’s study was a quarrel between dust and daylight. Scrolls threatened to emigrate. The wizard’s beard ran like a glacial river, grey threaded with something that wanted to be starlight. He was not, at that moment, studying the heavens.

“Edda. Rook. Come admire this.” He turned, theatrical as a curtain. The cloak around him was a captured sunset, constellations embroidered so they appeared to stroll. “It drinks twilight. Mystery, in garment form. Now: what urgent matter interrupts my sleeves?”

Edda, whose patience could have taught saints, kept her voice level. “I appear to have acquired the Sunstone Pendant by accident.”

Elmsworth’s eyes left the cloth for a blink. “Splendid. Weighty. A little plain. Take it to the Elder’s Circle. They will know.”

“Which circle?” Edda asked. “I have collected three legends already, and they disagree like poorly matched gloves.”

He waved, and gold fell off his cuff. “Legends are like badly cut cloaks. They fit no one and lead everyone into hedges. Follow the old paths. They have a habit of arriving. Now, if you will excuse me, the lunar embroidery is shy of a stitch.”

So they went down. The pendant hummed against Edda’s tunic, warm as a small animal with opinions. The paths were old enough. The people on them were not united. At a crossroads that tasted of pine and snowmelt, farmers waited with worry cut into their faces. Borin, their leader, spoke like unhewn stone. The pendant belonged in the Whispering Grove. The oldest oak said so in its bark, a script of knots and weather. Without it, he swore, no spring rain, no harvest worth the name. His people nodded as if rain were a committee decision. Edda listened. Rook listened harder. Neither corrected the oak.

Near the Chasm of Echoes, where wind practised being a ghost, artisans with calloused hands insisted otherwise. Tools still chalked their palms. The Sunstone belonged with the Sky-Singers, on the peak where eagles kept house. Only that song, in the thinnest air, could wake its true work. They spoke of life-giving power as if it were a commission. Edda did not argue. Argument, here, was a local sport with no off-season.

In a hamlet beside a waterfall that came down like a silver curtain, elders with eyes like used maps murmured a third certainty. They sat as if the benches had been assigned at the dawn of lists. The old texts were not shy. Bury it under the Great Fir. Anchor the valley. Keep the peace from drifting. One elder tapped the table twice, which in that hamlet counted as thunder.

Each group loved the mountain and disliked the other two. Mist, which had always been weather, began to smell of argument. Edda watched with a dry, tired humour. These were her people. They had forgotten how to hear.

Rook tapped her ear, once, twice, a third time: the valley’s own, the valley’s own, the valley’s own. He offered no speech. He offered stillness, which is rarer. Edda walked without answering anyone for a long while. She let the arguments fall behind her like loose stones. Prayer flags combed the firs into a chorus of colour, a whispering of cloth that had outlived several theories. Roots held the hill as if they had signed a contract. She saw, then, that none of the three loves were counterfeit. They were only incomplete. The Grove wanted beginning. The Singers wanted height. The Fir wanted not to be forgotten. All three, if you were not in a hurry, were the same mountain speaking in different rooms.

One blustery afternoon they stood on a precipice. Wind made a wild dance of Edda’s cloak. Rook nudged the pendant. A shaft of sun found the stone and threw a clean beam across the misted peaks, and the fragments clicked. The legends were not wrong. They were unfinished. The Sunstone was not a chair for one shrine. It was a task for many.

“I am calm,” Edda said, against the gale, “and I believe I know what must be done.”

She brought the leaders to a meadow as the mist thinned off the grass. She set the pendant in the middle. “Each of you has spoken truth. The Grove whispers beginnings. The Sky-Singers keep the height. The Fir holds the roots.”

Her plan did not choose. The Sunstone would travel, in season, from grove to peak to fir, always with a representative from each faction walking beside it. A pilgrimage. A yearly reminder that Aeridor was not three stories, but one with three rooms. She described the route as one describes a path already underfoot: not a decree, a habit waiting to start. In spring, the Grove. In high summer, the eagles’ air. In the first frost, the Fir’s dark. The stone would be accompanied, never owned.

Borin looked at the artisan and found, to his own surprise, a person instead of a fool. The artisan looked at the farmers and saw soil-wisdom instead of mud. The elders’ faces creased in a direction that was not age. The valley’s own, standing in one place, began to resemble a family that had remembered the way home.

Elmsworth appeared at the meadow’s edge, because vanity can also be punctual, and adjusted his cloak as if it had arranged the weather. “Ingenious. Shared endeavour. The aura of this garment, of course, did most of the diplomacy.”

Edda’s smile was small and dry. Rook, from a boulder, offered one caw that the valley chose to take as agreement. The pendant glowed with the less theatrical light of people who had stopped competing over a stone and started carrying it together.
characters: Edda (elf of air and assessing gaze), Rook (a raven who keeps mountain secrets), Elmsworth (a wizard far too pleased with his own cloak)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, highland fantasy adventure for teens
